Minimalism taken to the next level, Circa Infinity is one of these games which takes one premise and iterates over it again and again each time adding new conditions and restrictions to it, the general setting albeit stays the same. You're playing a trapped human always proceeding to an never ending cycle of circles

By touching a circle, you zoom in into the next layer, you will always start by running across the surface of the circle, as long that's the case you cannot jump, the goal is to find a loose piece on the circle and dive into it, after that, the process repeats. You are in the circle and have to touch a the smaller one inside of it, zooming into the next layer. Both the piece to dive in and the circle can move around or don't. its as different as the plethora of enemies you encounter throughout the game.

While the environment always stays the same the collection of enemies is what hinders you of just proceeding thoughtlessly. At first the game starts by placing immovable ones at at you, you simply have to jump over them, later on, they will start to move, fly and change layers. That's where it becomes tricky. Some enemies can even influence you although they are a layer above you, by having an extraordinaly large body, or simply phase outside the circle you are just about to move in.
This goes on after a while until you beat the chapter, yes this game is not endless, although the name and look might imply. 

There is another game inside the game called "Circa Affinity" this in fact IS an endless highscore game, like super hexagon where you have to dive in to as many layers a possible, this game fits too well in a highscore premise, so I suppose the developer patched that in later. It's good for longevity and definitely you can't stop once your started, it's pretty addicting.

After beating a chapter the game throws something entirely new at you, the concept extends slightly. The further you come, the more you have to think about your next step and eventually the game slowly turns into a puzzle-like game, where your approach becomes more important than your reflexes. 
The game absolutetly stays true to that concept till the end and so each time you think you accustomed to the overall premise which requries highest concentration, the game will only make your brain hurt more. 
Since I don't wanna spoiler the surprise I'm not going to tell you what exactly changes, all I can say is, if you think the game might become less complex over the time, nope. That's why perhaps some people could be turned off after the first 2 chapters of the game, it really comes down to preferences here, I appreciate the brave approach of the game becoming more convoluted without ever demanding highest precision over the course of the campaign. It becomes more complex, but not more demanding in its execution, maybe this is reassuring to hear for people that struggle.

One thing I have to mention I completely played each level deathless because the game rewards you for clearing levels without dying. The actual game is pretty forgiving, by dying you just have to replay the previous, however this can repeat if you die quickly in a row becoming more and more pushed back, but the game features layers without any enemies inbetween 4 or 5 circles in a row, which works like a safety net, so definitely it's not the hardest game for a normal playthrough, for a deathless playthrough however, it was definitely exhausting once I reached Chapter 3.

This is generally a game that shows how achievments can be implemented positively, working as incentives playing the game in odd fashion. There are creative achievments that restrict you to certain action like beat a level in chapter xy without stop moving, or beat a level without moving (only jump), accumulated times for each chapter, diverse circle affinity challenges and so on.
It's as fun as it's difficult trying to earn as much achievments as possible and it further adds to longevity.

All in all there is nothing I can really criticize about the game, it takes its concept, knows exactly what it wants to be and executes it in the most fitting way, exhausting all its potential, while never outstaying its welcome.
The unbelievable catchy music and mesmerizing visuals are just the icing on the cake and giving this game an unique identity.

So I can safely say, this is probably one the best and most fleshed out indie games on steam and I would consider it an artistic masterpiece.

Circa Infinity is a weird game. From the screenshots, it looks like... chaos, but as for its genre, it looks like an endless runner, but it's actually a puzzle-platformer. It's definitely one of my favorite platformers.

Circa Infinity is split into 5 parts with 10 levels and a boss each. Each part has you approach levels differently (ex. instead of one character, how about two?) and each level throws a new puzzle/challenge at you. I would say the main appeal would be the craziness of the visuals and the conciseness of the levels. The first part (or two) is more of a tutorial and not super interesting, but carry on, for the later levels are much more interesting.

Even if Circa Infinity is one of my favorite platformers, it has its issues. For one, the puzzling aspect of the platforming. Enemy movement and circle ascending (that the right word?) is clearly the main puzzle element, and I don't have issues with that. I have issues with the parts with two players: which circle sector you enter first can force a death if you want to continue. (For example, two enemies on either side of the sector: they prevent you from moving the other character to the other sector.)
I also encountered a bug on the fourth boss. Starting the boss battle, the left half rotates while the right half doesn't, but dying will fix this (though it certainly is a great challenge, if you want to attempt). I think there were some other minor bugs but that was the most obvious one I remember.
My biggest issue would be the menu: [i] why the heck are there no words?! [/i] When I first booted up the game, I accidentally entered the endless runner mode (called Circle Affinity) and spent more than I would like to admit finding my way back. Circle Affinity also has very annoying visual changes: sometimes the background will change to white, but the circle and character are white, so either you're great at remembering where everything is or you have to wait.

The achievements are another way to challenge yourself with unique puzzles, like don't jump for a level or only run in one direction for another. Of course, you could forget that and just focus on completing the level as fast as possible.

Circa Infinity is one of my favorite platformers. The 2-player circle ascending issue I mentioned above prevents me from recommending this game to all, but the game is still an excellent platformer. It can get really difficult, especially if you're aiming for 100% completion. I recommend it to all fans of the platformer genre.

This game is Braid meets Super Hexagon

I was immediately hooked. This may be the best puzzle-platformer I've played since Braid, except instead of a narrative experience, all levels take place in concentric circles that you can walk on, either inside or outside. The challenge and variety then comes from avoiding the different demons that have their own behaviors and properties, to be able to jump to the next circle. You then progress into increasingly difficult concentric circles until you reach the level goal. After a series of levels, there's a unique boss fight that uses the same circle jumping methods. It's a very mechanically pure game, so if you enjoy that type of games, you may like this.

As if that wasn't enough, there's a secondary game mode called Circle Affinity that's puts less emphasis on nevigation puzzles and instead on pure twitch reflexes, as you have a time limit to jump to the next circle before the outer circles close into you. And it features unlockable color palettes à la Downwell, and I'm a sucker for those.

Oh, and the soundtrack is great!

Circa Infinity is a decent puzzle-platformer wrapped into a very striking and thought-blending aesthetic. The game's literally all about running inside and outside circles, with a single trick for progressing (and survival) being well-timed jumps. Mechanically the game's actually not too far from the likes of 'The Impossible Game', as you're mostly expected to progress through every level as fast as possible without dying (atleast all of the achievements point towards that ideal). There's some variety [i](apart from the ever-increasing level complexity and enemy/obstacle variety)[/i] that comes in the form of boss stages and achievement-related alterate progression styles, but after the game's initial visual rush wears off it reveals itself as another 'execution test'-type of action puzzle game. I don't dislike that, and neither the very speedrun-friendly design of the game, but there's not enough technical freedom to keep me invested long-term. I do think the game's worth its price as a solid few-hour experience, but it lacks a lasting enjoyment factor.

Circa Infinity (& Affinity). What a game.

Circa Infinity is a puzzle mode featuring 5 worlds. As you progress, you will encounter worlds that introduce new game concepts, especially in worlds 4 & 5. If you aim for completion, I advise you to take your time and carefully analyze the movement patterns. However, if you're an achievement hunter (like me), perfect your hand-eye coordination, your visual memory layout of the levels, and your commitment into seeing this through to the end. I didn't receive a proper warning, so I'll warn you now: if you lack any of the three points I've listed above, DON'T go for Circa Infinity achievements. 


Circa Affinity closely resembles Super Hexagon, a mobile, and more recently on Steam, game developed by Terry Cavanagh. Both are endless. Both have locked stages with different game mechanics and you can only advance if you bypass the game's 'threshold' for that stage. Also, each stage have their repeating patterns in an endless sequence of patterns.

This is the part where I will claim thatt Circa Affinity is more brutal than Super Hexagon. For Super Hexagon, you only need to keep in mind where your arrow points and looking ahead for the next pattern. You need to pay attention to a number of things in Circa Affinity:
[list]
    [*]Direction of avatar movement (counterclockwise or clockwise)
    [*]Direction of floor movement (counterclockwise, clockwise, or stationary {sometimes, wedges can move in unique patterns)
    [*]Direction of enemy movement, whether ground or air(counterclockwise, clockwise, or stationary {also special condition enemies})
    [*]Direction of next floor orbit (counterclockwise, clockwise, or stationary)
    [*]Kaleidoscope animations (very distracting).
[/list]

As you can probably tell, hunting for Circa Infinity achievements is as demanding, if not more, as excelling in Circa Affinity. Before I forget, yes, if you feel your brain's going to leak from your skull, take frequent breaks, or stop, playing Circa Infinity. I knew I had to, moreso during the Speedrun.

Sure, I'm reviewing this game after playing it for less than an hour. BUT! It is already one of my favorite games. It is so simple, repetitive, and downright addicting. I will go to work tomorrow seeing circles. And the soundtrack just keeps it pumping. One caveat: the control scheme takes some getting used to. I really have to think about which direction will move me which way, which adds complexity especially in the Circle Affinity mode. I appreciate the option between whether I want to play a structured platformer which forgives mistakes (Circa Infinity mode) and a progressively difficult arcade game with instadeath (Circle Affinity mode).

Overall, I appreciate this aesthetic, and it is a game I want people to watch me play.
